newsitem.title: RUSSIA: IMF methods said ignoring Russian economic reality.
newsitem.headline: IMF methods said ignoring Russian economic reality.

text.p: Western-style inflation rates and a narrowing budget deficit should be good news for a team of IMF experts reviewing Russia's economic performance this week.

But some analysts say the figures take little note of large parts of the economy operating outside the cash sector. Firms delay tax, wage and other payments, and existing economic models do not give a full picture of the Russian economic scene.

"There is always a temptation to...use a simplified vision of economy -- a sort of virtual reality -- which has as much to do with the real economy as a computer game has with life," Sevodnya economic commentator Mikhail Leontev wrote this week.
"In Russia the forecasts built on the basis of well-proven recipes of economic thought just do not work."
The reassuring images of economic stabilisation are based on Russia's record low inflation rate and the rouble's performance within a sloping corridor set by the Russian central bank.

Consumer prices fell 0.2 percent in August, the first decline since Russia began its economic reforms in January 1992. Double-digit monthly inflation was common in the early years of the economic transformation.
Those high inflation rates helped foster a mentality of non-payments as firms and individuals delayed paying bills because they knew the value would go down month by month.

The attitude still exists in the new, low-inflation Russia, where workers strike because they have not been paid for months and the government, itself a debtor to firms and regions, struggles to raise tax revenue.

Economists say companies have money, but prefer to use it on the high-yielding market for government securities than for mundane things like paying bills. Annual yields on short-term government securities are just over 60 percent.
Official figures show that wealthy sectors like gas and non-ferrous metals are behind on payments to the government and to other creditors.

July figures show that the gas sector, 95 percent under the thumb of monopolist producer Gazprom, owed 4.7 trillion roubles to the government and 7.8 trillion to its suppliers. The machine building sector owes the government 17.3 trillion roubles.

"The key to success or failure is whether there are any holy cows or not," said Jochen Wermuth, head of the Finance Ministry's Economic Expert Group, referring to companies like Gazprom, which have traditionally been viewed as above the law.
"If there are no holy cows, revenues will come this autumn."
He said officials were determined to get tough on companies which did not pay their bills.

Finance ministry figures released on Thursday showed that the budget deficit narrowed to 6.3 percent of gross domestic product in August, from 6.6 percent in July, using IMF methods of calculating both the deficit and GDP.

The IMF, which has backed Russian economic reforms with a $10 billion three-year loan, last month set a new 1996 target for the Russian budget deficit of 5.25 percent of gross domestic product. The previous target was four percent.
The IMF delayed paying the July tranche of the loan because it was worried about low tax revenues and a wide budget deficit.
A delegation is spending most of this week in Moscow and will report back to Washington in time for the IMF's early October annual meetings.
Wermuth said tax collection, especially VAT collection, had been rising in August.
He said new regulations that firms pay VAT and excise duties when they deliver goods should boost revenues further.
Firms previously paid tax only when they received payment for the goods they supplied.
($ 1 = 5,400 roubles)
